clue.text: What next — cribbed from Macbeth, Tomkin ?

definitions.text: What next — cribbed from Macbeth, Tomkin ?

parts.words: What next — cribbed from Macbeth, Tomkin
parts.note: Macbeth, hearing Fleance has escaped, says he is now confined, cribbed and shut in: the word that sits beside 'cribbed' in that famous line

explanation.surface: Someone asks a classmate called Tomkin what line comes next in a crib of Macbeth.
explanation.walkthrough: Macbeth's line is "But now I am cabin'd, cribb'd, confin'd, bound in to saucy doubts and fears"; the clue asks for the word paired with 'cribbed' there.
explanation.definitionFit: Shut up in a small room, like a ship's berth, is the sense Macbeth gives the word, alongside cribbed and confined.

clue.text: Standard forms of :Turkish town planning ?

parts.note: standard means a flag: the Turkish flag bears a curved moon emblem, and town planners lay out curved terraces of the same shape

explanation.surface: Turkey's usual approach to planning its towns.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Standard' reads as 'usual', but it is a flag; British towns have curved streets of houses called by the same name.
explanation.definitionFit: Curved moon shapes appear on the Turkish flag and are also curved rows of houses.

clue.text: Such parsnips being 'too good for words ?.

definitions.text: Such parsnips being 'too good for words ?.

parts.words: Such parsnips being 'too good for words
parts.note: the proverb says fine words butter no parsnips; parsnips that have been dressed with fat were never served by words

explanation.surface: Parsnips so delicious they leave you speechless.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'fine words butter no parsnips' means talk achieves nothing; parsnips with butter on them must have had something better than words.
explanation.definitionFit: Coated or dressed with the dairy spread, as the proverb's parsnips never are by mere words.

clue.text: See here, Mrs Bull is no slattern

definitions.text: See here, Mrs Bull is no slattern

parts.words: See here, Mrs Bull is no slattern
parts.note: Mrs Bull is a cow, neat being an old word for cattle as well as meaning tidy; her shed is a tidy house

explanation.surface: A neighbour insists that Mrs Bull keeps a tidy home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Neat' is an archaic word for cattle, so a cowshed bears that name, and a tidy woman keeps a neat house.
explanation.definitionFit: An old word for a cowshed, a building where cattle are kept.

clue.text: Wet bob. Donald.

definitions.meaning: to bob down under water and get wet
Donald is Walt Disney's cartoon bird

explanation.walkthrough: At Eton a 'wet bob' is a boy who rows; here the words are read literally as a quick dip into water.
explanation.definitionFit: To dip briefly under water, and the surname of Disney's sailor-suited cartoon character.

clue.text: Cattle twitch perforce ?

definitions.note: read as 'by force': an adverb standing for an adjective about motion and force, hence the question mark

parts.note: kine is the old plural of cow, meaning cattle
a tic is a nervous twitch

explanation.surface: Cows that twitch because they have to.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perforce' normally means 'necessarily', but split as 'per force' it suggests something brought about by force or motion.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes motion and the energy of moving bodies, the result of force acting on them.

clue.text: May it please his Majesty to entrain here? No!

definitions.text: May it please his Majesty to entrain here? No

parts.words: May it please his Majesty to entrain here? No
parts.note: a courtier asks whether the monarch will board at this station, and the answer is no because he would be angry, the station's name read as the ruler being annoyed

explanation.surface: A courtier asks if the King would like to board his train at this station.
explanation.walkthrough: King's Cross is a major London railway terminus; read as 'the king is cross', it shows why the answer to the courtier is no.
explanation.definitionFit: A London mainline railway terminus, whose name also suggests an annoyed monarch.

clue.text: Poor Edward Marshal is outside

indicators.note: the marshal's name is outside, wrapped around the short name

parts.note: Michel Ney was one of Napoleon's marshals
Ed is short for Edward

explanation.surface: Poor Edward Marshal has been left out in the cold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Edward Marshal' looks like one man's name; Michel Ney was a marshal of France under Napoleon, and 'is outside' wraps him round the short Edward.
explanation.definitionFit: Poor and lacking money or necessities are synonyms.

clue.text: Male adornments to prepare for three legged race

definitions.meaning: ornamental pins worn on a man's necktie

definitions.text: to prepare for three legged race
definitions.meaning: pins is slang for legs, and partners in a three-legged race tie their inner legs together

explanation.walkthrough: 'Pins' is British slang for legs.
explanation.definitionFit: Decorative pins for a cravat, and binding legs together before a three-legged race.

clue.text: Boy gets pass in

parts.note: a col is a mountain pass

explanation.surface: A lad is given a pass to go in.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a common boy's name.

clue.text: .No --s, no vacations, and diet unparalleled at Dotheboys Hall

definitions.text: .No --s, no vacations, and diet unparalleled at Dotheboys Hall

parts.words: No --s, no vacations, and diet unparalleled at Dotheboys Hall
parts.note: the blank is filled from Squeers's advertisement for his Yorkshire school in Dickens's Nicholas Nickleby, which promised parents no additional charges

explanation.surface: A quotation from a boarding-school prospectus with one word blanked out.
explanation.walkthrough: Dotheboys Hall is Wackford Squeers's cruel school in Nicholas Nickleby; its advert boasted of no additional fees and no holidays, and the diet was unparalleled because it was so meagre.
explanation.definitionFit: Additional charges added to school fees are what Squeers promised parents they would not pay.

clue.text: Good-bye dance for one long at sea

parts.note: a conge (congé) is a formal leave-taking or dismissal
a reel is a lively Scottish dance

explanation.surface: A farewell dance is held for someone who has been away at sea a long time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one long at sea' looks like a long-serving sailor, but it describes a long fish living in the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: This large marine fish has a long snake-like body and lives in the sea.

clue.text: Where the public' take tots

parts.note: tots suggests small drinks taken at a public house, but here they are small children left at a public day nursery

explanation.surface: A pub where drinkers knock back their tots of whisky.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'tot' is both a small measure of spirits and a small child, so the drinking scene turns into parents dropping off toddlers.
explanation.definitionFit: A day nursery is a place where young children are looked after while parents work.

clue.text: Old empire man in role of modern belligerent

parts.note: as means in the capacity or role of
a Syrian, from a modern state then at war with its neighbours

explanation.surface: A man from an ancient empire is cast as a present-day fighter.
explanation.walkthrough: When the puzzle appeared Syria was among the Arab states at war with Israel, hence 'modern belligerent'.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of the ancient Mesopotamian empire centred on Nineveh.

clue.text: Least rubicund form of R.A. in this: composer.

parts.note: rubicund means ruddy, so least ruddy is the most pallid

indicators.note: form as in a new shape, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: RA, as written

explanation.surface: The palest work by a Royal Academician shows a composer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'form of' rearranges R.A. with 'in'; 'this' just links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina was the great Italian Renaissance writer of church music.

clue.text: Liqueur giving you an odd nutty flavour

indicators.note: odd means strange or irregular, so these letters are put in an unusual order

explanation.surface: A liqueur with a curiously nutty taste.
explanation.walkthrough: Rearranging YOUAN gives a brandy liqueur flavoured with fruit kernels, which explains the 'nutty flavour' at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a brandy-based cordial flavoured with apricot or peach kernels, giving an almond taste.

clue.text: Go-getter who does not agree it is better to travel hopefully

definitions.text: Go-getter who does not agree it is better to travel hopefully

parts.words: Go-getter who does not agree it is better to travel hopefully
parts.note: R. L. Stevenson wrote that to travel hopefully is a better thing than to arrive; an ambitious upstart cares only about getting there

explanation.surface: A thrusting type who dismisses the old saying about travelling hopefully.
explanation.walkthrough: The French word for an upstart literally means 'one who arrives', so this person disagrees with Stevenson and values arrival.
explanation.definitionFit: An ambitious social climber or upstart, from the French for someone who has arrived.

clue.text: Describes what's left of one U.S. soldier embraced by a Roman virgin

indicators.note: the soldier and one are held inside the Roman virgin's word

parts.note: a vestal virgin served the goddess Vesta in ancient Rome
I is the Roman numeral for one
GI is an American soldier

explanation.surface: An American soldier is hugged by a Roman priestess.
explanation.walkthrough: 'embraced by' places one and the GI inside the Roman priestess; vestal virgins tended the sacred fire of Vesta.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective applies to a remnant or trace, something remaining of what once existed.

clue.text: Architect's work bringing a peerage ?

definitions.meaning: an architect draws a flat view of a building's face
being raised to the House of Lords is a promotion upwards

explanation.walkthrough: 'bringing' links the two senses.
explanation.definitionFit: An architect's drawing of a building's face, and a raising in rank such as to the nobility.

clue.text: Making no bones about being a worm

definitions.text: Making no bones about being a worm

parts.words: Making no bones about being a worm
parts.note: to make no bones is to be frank, but a worm literally has no backbone, and a weak person is a worm too

explanation.surface: Someone openly admits they are a contemptible coward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Making no bones about' reads as 'openly admitting', but it describes having no backbone at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacking a backbone, both literally like an invertebrate and figuratively as a weak, cowardly person.

clue.text: Slovenly nit, and graceless — you have no right to be here

definitions.text: you have no right to be here

indicators.note: slovenly means untidy, so these letters are put in disorder

parts.note: rude means lacking grace or manners

explanation.surface: An untidy, ill-mannered nitwit is told they are not welcome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slovenly' scrambles the nit; the definition is a phrase describing what an intruder is told.
explanation.definitionFit: To barge in where one is not welcome or entitled to be.

clue.text: Witch's bark Aleppo-bound

parts.note: in Macbeth the first witch, whose victim's husband is gone to Aleppo, says she will sail there in a strainer

explanation.surface: A witch's boat setting out for the Syrian city of Aleppo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bark' is an old word for a boat, not a dog's noise or a tree's skin; the witch in Macbeth Act 1 says "in a sieve I'll thither sail".
explanation.definitionFit: A mesh strainer is the unlikely vessel Shakespeare's witch chooses for her voyage.

clue.text: Make shift to get lean and be graceful

indicators.note: to make something shift is to move it around, rearranging these letters

explanation.surface: Moving about to get slim and be graceful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make shift' rearranges GET and LEAN; 'makeshift' would suggest improvised, a false trail.
explanation.definitionFit: Stylish and refined in movement or appearance.

clue.text: Thongs for odd chatels

indicators.note: odd means peculiar, telling us to rearrange the letters of the word that follows

parts.note: chattels, personal possessions; printed with one T

explanation.surface: Leather straps traded for strange bits of property.
explanation.walkthrough: The page prints 'chatels', one T short; the anagram needs CHATTELS, whose letters rearrange to the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Latchets are the leather straps or laces that fasten a shoe or sandal.

clue.text: Nothing impious escaped this old master's mouth'

definitions.text: Nothing impious escaped this old master's mouth'

parts.words: Nothing impious escaped this old master's mouth'
parts.note: the mouth is the lip and nothing impious means it was pi, slang for pious, giving the Florentine painter's name

explanation.surface: An old master who never said anything blasphemous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pi' is old British school slang for pious; the lip being pi gives the name of Fra Filippo Lippi, Renaissance painter.
explanation.definitionFit: Filippo Lippi and his son Filippino were Florentine painters of the Renaissance.

clue.text: Godiva's anti-tax dispensation

parts.note: Lady Godiva rode naked through Coventry to get a tax lifted, so what she dispensed with was her riding dress

explanation.surface: Lady Godiva is granted an exemption from tax.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dispensation' looks like an official exemption, but it is the thing she dispensed with: her riding clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: A riding outfit, the clothing she did without on her ride.

clue.text: Flicks on' here .

parts.note: flicks reads as a verb, switching something on, but it is slang for films, which are on at this place

explanation.surface: Someone flicks a light switch on right here.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flicks' is informal for films, especially British; 'on' means being shown.
explanation.definitionFit: A picture house is where films are shown to an audience.

clue.text: Little woman starts building Thebes

indicators.note: building as constructing, so these letters are put together in a new order
only the start of the city's name is used, its ending dropped

explanation.surface: A small woman begins constructing an ancient city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'starts' keeps THEB, the beginning of Thebes, and 'building' rearranges it.
explanation.definitionFit: Beth March is one of the four sisters in Louisa May Alcott's novel Little Women.

clue.text: It sounds straight

parts.note: sounds suggests making a noise, but to sound is also to measure the depth of water with a weighted cord that hangs vertical

explanation.surface: Something sounds honest and direct.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sounds' here means takes soundings of depth, and the weighted cord also shows a true vertical, so it is straight.
explanation.definitionFit: A cord with a weight on the end is used by builders to find a true vertical and by sailors to measure depth.

clue.text: One artist has backing of a measure of intelligence, foreign to us

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
RA is a Royal Academician, an artist

indicators.note: backing means the following piece is read backwards

parts.note: IQ, intelligence quotient

explanation.surface: An artist backed by a gauge of brainpower that is alien to us.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing of' turns only the intelligence measure round; 'foreign to us' means from abroad, as a definition of a nationality.
explanation.definitionFit: A person from a Middle Eastern country is a foreigner to British solvers.

clue.text: Sort 'of train, that 'is, 'won't: go of itself

indicators.note: sort as a verb means arrange, so these letters are reordered

parts.note: ie, id est, means that is

explanation.surface: A train that will not start by itself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sort of' rearranges TRAIN plus IE.
explanation.definitionFit: The tendency of a body at rest to stay at rest, so it never starts moving unaided.

clue.text: Dancers pelted here ?

parts.note: the Cornish town of the Furry Dance has a name that sounds like the frozen pellets that pelt people in a storm

explanation.surface: Somewhere dancers are pelted with missiles.
explanation.walkthrough: Helston, a town in Cornwall, England, is famous for its Floral (Furry) Dance each May; its name sounds like 'hailstone'.
explanation.definitionFit: This Cornish market town holds the Flora Day dance through its streets every year.
